terms.definition: Reinforcing steel bars embedded in concrete to provide tensile strength.
terms.whyItMatters: You verify spacing, cover (distance from surface), and tie placement to ensure structural integrity before the pour.
terms.armyAnalog: Like ammunition supply verification — correct quantities, correct placement, correct documentation before the mission starts.
commonMistakes: Assuming placement is correct without checking the drawings

terms.definition: The process of placing liquid concrete into formwork to cure into a structural element.
terms.whyItMatters: A critical inspection point — affects structural integrity, schedule, and budget if it goes wrong.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a live-fire exercise — once it starts, there's no undo. Everything has to be verified beforehand.
commonMistakes: Starting finishes before proper cure time

terms.definition: Temporary molds used to shape and hold concrete in place until it cures.
terms.whyItMatters: You verify dimensions, plumb, and bracing before the pour — errors here are locked into the structure permanently.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a range safety fan — the boundaries have to be exactly right before anything happens inside them.

terms.definition: Steel beams, columns, and connections that form a building's structural skeleton.
terms.whyItMatters: You verify bolt torque, weld quality, and plumb/alignment against structural drawings.
terms.armyAnalog: Like verifying a bridge classification before crossing — the load path has to be exactly what the engineer specified.

terms.definition: Plumb means perfectly vertical; level means perfectly horizontal. Both are checked with lasers or levels.
terms.whyItMatters: Out-of-tolerance elements compound as construction progresses — a small error on floor 1 becomes a big one by floor 10.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a zeroed weapon sight — small errors at the point of origin become large errors downrange.

terms.definition: The base structural element that transfers building loads into the soil.
terms.whyItMatters: Footing depth, width, and rebar placement are foundational — literally. Errors here affect everything built above.
terms.armyAnalog: Like establishing a secure base of operations — everything else depends on this being right.

terms.definition: A formal question submitted to the design team when drawings are unclear, conflicting, or missing information.
terms.whyItMatters: RFIs create a documented paper trail and prevent field guessing on design intent — guessing wrong can mean expensive rework.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a request for clarification up the chain of command before executing an ambiguous order.
commonMistakes: Not RFI-ing an ambiguity and guessing instead
Vague RFI language that generates a vague answer

terms.definition: Documentation (product data, shop drawings, samples) a subcontractor submits for architect/engineer approval before fabrication or installation.
terms.whyItMatters: You track submittal status to make sure trades aren't installing unapproved materials — which can force teardown and re-installation.
terms.armyAnalog: Like getting a plan approved before execution — you don't move out until higher headquarters signs off.

terms.definition: A formal, agreed-upon modification to the contract scope, cost, or schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: You document field conditions that drive change orders — accurate records protect the project's budget and schedule.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a fragmentary order (FRAGO) that modifies the original operations order mid-mission.

terms.definition: A list of incomplete or defective items that must be corrected before a phase or project is accepted as complete.
terms.whyItMatters: You generate and track punch items daily — the goal is to "punch as you go" instead of a massive list at the end.
terms.armyAnalog: Like an after-action review (AAR) findings list — specific, assigned, and tracked to closure.
commonMistakes: Letting punch items pile up instead of correcting as you go
Vague punch descriptions with no location or owner

terms.definition: A formal daily record of site activity: weather, manpower, work performed, deliveries, and issues.
terms.whyItMatters: Daily reports are the project's legal and historical record — they're used to resolve disputes and delay claims months later.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a daily situation report (SITREP) — factual, timestamped, and used for both current awareness and future record.

terms.definition: Mechanical, Electrical, and Plumbing — the three primary building systems trades.
terms.whyItMatters: MEP coordination is one of the most common sources of conflict and rework on a job site — systems have to physically fit in the same space.
terms.armyAnalog: Like coordinating fires, maneuver, and logistics — three different systems that all have to occupy the same space and time without colliding.

terms.definition: The stage where MEP systems (pipes, conduit, ductwork) are installed inside walls/ceilings before they're closed up.
terms.whyItMatters: This is your last chance to inspect before the work is hidden behind drywall or ceiling tile — mistakes found later mean demolition.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a pre-combat inspection — the last check before everything is committed and can't be easily undone.
commonMistakes: Approving rough-in before all trades have completed their portion

terms.definition: The process of resolving physical clashes between mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems before installation, often using 3D BIM models.
terms.whyItMatters: Uncoordinated MEP causes field clashes — expensive, schedule-killing rework when two systems try to occupy the same space.
terms.armyAnalog: Like deconflicting airspace and ground maneuver — done in planning so it never becomes a problem in execution.

terms.definition: Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning — the mechanical systems that control a building's climate.
terms.whyItMatters: On a data center, HVAC (cooling specifically) is mission-critical infrastructure, not just comfort — servers fail without it.
terms.armyAnalog: Like environmental control on a deployed command post — critical infrastructure, not a comfort item.

terms.definition: Electrical equipment used to control, protect, and isolate electrical equipment (breakers, switches, fuses).
terms.whyItMatters: Data centers are power-dense; switchgear installation tolerances and testing are heavily scrutinized.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a power distribution point at a forward operating base — critical, high-consequence infrastructure.

terms.definition: The sequence of dependent tasks that determines the shortest possible project duration — any delay here delays the whole project.
terms.whyItMatters: You need to know which tasks are on the critical path so you can flag delays immediately instead of after the fact.
terms.armyAnalog: Like the decisive point in an operation — the one thing that, if delayed, delays everything downstream.

terms.definition: A short-term (typically 2-3 week) detailed schedule that breaks the master schedule into actionable near-term tasks.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the schedule you actually work from day to day — it's where trade sequencing conflicts get caught early.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a weekly training or operations schedule that translates a broader campaign plan into executable near-term tasks.

terms.definition: A significant, fixed point in the schedule marking the completion of a major phase (e.g., "structure topped out").
terms.whyItMatters: Milestones are what the Owner and PM track most closely — you help ensure the underlying work supports hitting them.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a phase line or objective in an operations order — a fixed marker of progress everyone tracks against.

terms.definition: The amount of time a task can be delayed without impacting the overall project schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding which tasks have float (and which don't) tells you what's safe to flex and what needs immediate escalation.
terms.armyAnalog: Like slack time built into a movement plan — useful, but it runs out fast once consumed.

terms.definition: The setup phase where a contractor establishes site infrastructure (trailers, fencing, utilities) before construction begins.
terms.whyItMatters: A clean mobilization sets the tone for the whole project — site logistics planned poorly here cause friction for months.
terms.armyAnalog: Like establishing a forward operating base — the setup determines how smoothly everything after it runs.

terms.definition: Quality Assurance / Quality Control — the processes that verify work meets specifications before and after installation.
terms.whyItMatters: This is a core part of the FE role — you are the field's frontline QA/QC check.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a standards inspection — verifying execution matches the published standard, every time, not just when someone's watching.

terms.definition: A standardized checklist used to verify specific installation criteria before work is covered or moves to the next phase.
terms.whyItMatters: Checklists ensure consistency — you're not relying on memory to catch every required check across dozens of similar inspections.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a pre-combat inspection (PCI) checklist — the same standard applied every single time, no shortcuts.

terms.definition: Verifying installed work matches the project specifications (materials, methods, tolerances) laid out in the contract documents.
terms.whyItMatters: Spec is the legal standard the work is measured against — "looks fine" isn't the same as "meets spec."
terms.armyAnalog: Like verifying equipment serviceability against the technical manual, not just visual inspection.

terms.definition: A formal document identifying work that does not meet specifications, requiring a documented correction plan.
terms.whyItMatters: NCRs create accountability and a paper trail for how a quality issue was found, fixed, and verified.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a deficiency report on equipment — documented, tracked, and closed out formally, not just fixed quietly.

terms.definition: The distance between reinforcing steel and the outer surface of the concrete.
terms.whyItMatters: Insufficient cover leads to steel corrosion and structural failure over time — it's a precise, code-mandated measurement.
terms.armyAnalog: Like maintaining proper standoff distance — a specific, non-negotiable measurement for a structural reason.

terms.definition: Drawings updated to reflect the actual final installed conditions, which often differ slightly from the original design.
terms.whyItMatters: You help maintain accurate as-builts — they're critical for the Owner's future maintenance and any future renovation.
terms.armyAnalog: Like updating a range card after actually occupying the position — the real conditions, not just the plan.

terms.definition: The contract section covering project-wide items: site logistics, safety, temporary facilities, and administration.
terms.whyItMatters: General requirements shape day-to-day site operations — badging, parking, laydown areas, and safety protocols all live here.
terms.armyAnalog: Like standard operating procedures (SOPs) that govern how the whole operation runs, independent of the specific mission.

terms.definition: Detailed fabrication drawings produced by a subcontractor or supplier showing exactly how they will build/install their scope.
terms.whyItMatters: You compare shop drawings to design intent and field conditions to catch conflicts before fabrication.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a detailed operations order annex — the specific execution plan derived from the higher-level intent.

terms.definition: The process of physically marking building elements' exact locations on site using survey equipment, based on drawings.
terms.whyItMatters: This is a core daily FE task — a layout error compounds through every subsequent trade that builds off it.
terms.armyAnalog: Like establishing grid coordinates for a range or objective — precision here prevents everything downstream from being wrong.
commonMistakes: Not verifying layout against two independent reference points

terms.definition: The process of maintaining moisture and temperature in concrete after pouring so it gains strength properly.
terms.whyItMatters: Loading or working on concrete before it's cured can cause cracking or structural weakness.
terms.armyAnalog: Like a mandatory stand-down period after intense exertion — skipping it causes failures later.

terms.definition: An immediate, mandatory work stoppage to address an identified safety hazard before work resumes.
terms.whyItMatters: As an FE, you have the authority — and responsibility — to call a stand-down when you see an immediate hazard.
terms.armyAnalog: Like calling "cease fire" immediately when a safety violation is observed — no hesitation, no exceptions.
